extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians (aspiring and professional), comedy performers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and tactics for stand-up comedians on what to do when a set is failing (bombing), including how to respond onstage, when to bail, how to learn from it, and how to adapt to different rooms/situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that you're bombing
rubrics_metrics.description: Call out the fact you are bombing so the audience knows you know what's happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Always acknowledge that you’re bombing in the moment. Say something, anything, so the audience knows that you know that you’re bombing.” — Erica Rhodes. This takes pressure off everyone and can sometimes turn the situation around (e.g., audience members sympathizing afterward).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make fun of the bombing (or the audience) — but not too much
rubrics_metrics.description: Use self-referential or audience-directed humor to defuse silence, but avoid blaming the audience or overdoing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “If you’re bombing, make fun of it, but not too much. Sometimes it’s good to make fun of the audience. Just don’t blame them with a ‘What? You guys don’t like [fill in the blank with the topic of your joke here]??’” — Matt Braunger. Avoid alienating language that accuses or shames the crowd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemptive self-judgment / admit failure quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: State you’re bombing before the crowd judges you; be the one to judge yourself first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “When I bomb I let the crowd know before they do that I’m bombing. Nobody can judge me faster than I can judge myself.” — Andy Kindler. This contrasts with pretending things are fine and can speed up moving on from failing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bail on failing material quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandon bits that aren’t landing as soon as you recognize they aren’t working rather than trying to force them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Andy Kindler: “I like to bail on the material as fast as possible.” Fast exits from failing bits reduce time spent sinking and open opportunities to pivot or end gracefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep rhythm, confidence, and avoid rushing when bombing
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain performance tempo and stage confidence; do not speed up or panic, which usually worsens the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Keeping your rhythm and confidence and being consistent is the best thing you can do. One of the hardest things is to not start rushing and getting nervous when you are bombing. That usually makes the situation worse.” — Shane Mauss. Consistency can help a cold room warm up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bombing as material and a learning opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat bombing as valuable feedback: learn from it, write more, and incorporate lessons into new material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Bombing is actually a gift. That’s when you learn the most.” — Erica Rhodes. “Take it on board and write more.” — Greg Proops. Use failed performances to refine jokes and identify weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you’re being paid, do your time; if not, decide whether to stay
rubrics_metrics.description: When booked and paid, fulfill the set even if it’s rough; unpaid spots can be abandoned if conditions are poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “If you’re being paid, do your time. If you’re not being paid, evaluate whether you want to subject yourself to the silence or scorn and bail if you want.” — Jackie Kashian. Consider contractual/professional obligations when deciding to continue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t waste energy trying to win over stubborn hecklers or hostile crowd members
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid over-exerting to win over people who clearly won’t respond; maintain pride and defiance instead of begging for laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Don’t try too hard to win over stubborn jerks that aren’t giving you any love. Stay proud and defiant…” — Jesse Elias. Pick your battles; some audience members aren’t persuadable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt material and expectations to room size and technical conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize when a venue, crowd size, or sound setup makes your usual material ineffective and adjust accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brooks Wheelan’s festival set failed partly because he hadn’t considered the enormous crowd and sound delay: jokes were heard with a half-second lag. Advice: think about sound, scale, and format before scaling up material that works in smaller rooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exit gracefully when the situation is untenable
rubrics_metrics.description: If the set is irretrievable, end it cleanly and with a short exit line rather than escalating or arguing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brooks Wheelan: when students walked on and cut him off, he said, “Enjoy Ludacris” and left. A calm, witty exit avoids confrontation and preserves professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid post-show public fights about the bombing (don’t escalate online)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not prolong the failure by engaging in public arguments (e.g., Twitter wars) after the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brooks Wheelan described getting into a Twitter war with the college and later realizing it was a terrible idea. Let the set end and move on instead of amplifying the incident online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t storm off in childish anger; preserve professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving the stage angrily is unprofessional and self-sabotaging; learn from such mistakes and commit not to repeat them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allen Strickland Williams recalled storming off early on and called it childish and petty, promising never to do it again. Maintain composure even on rough nights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some situations require reading the room — sometimes acknowledge, sometimes don’t
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no one-size-fits-all: sometimes calling attention to the coldness helps, sometimes it makes it worse; develop judgment through experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shane Mauss: “Sometimes it’s good to acknowledge the situation, sometimes that only makes people more uncomfortable. Every situation is different. You get better at reading it with experience.” Training your audience-reading skill is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain perspective: bombing is temporary and can strengthen you
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember that bombing stings but is fleeting; the next show is another chance and bombing can make you a stronger performer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening paragraphs and multiple comics stress that bombing heals by the next night and can result in great stories. Allen Strickland Williams: “Enjoy it!... There’s always another show.” Use this outlook to reduce fear of failure.
